title: Physics-Based TCAD Modeling of Nanowire Cryotrons with Coupled Superconducting and Thermal Dynamics
summary: Nanowire cryotrons (nTrons) provide gate-controlled superconducting switching, current gain, and high-impedance outputs for cryogenic computing, detector readout, and superconductor-semiconductor interfaces. We develop a physics-based Sentaurus TCAD framework that couples time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau dynamics, separate electron and phonon energy equations, and mixed-mode circuit simulation. Superconducting terminal-current corrections connect the custom solver to the native electrical solution, linking local suppression of superconductivity, heating and cooling, and current redistribution in the external circuit. To our knowledge, this is the first Sentaurus-based mixed-mode TCAD implementation for nTrons. We calibrate the model against experimental switching data at six gate currents using a single parameter set. The model achieves an RMS load-current error below 1 $μ$A outside the switching region and switching-current differences of about 1 $μ$A or less. Simulations show that a center gate gives the highest switching sensitivity, while a drain-side gate gives the largest post-switch resistance. Narrower channels switch at lower currents and exhibit higher resistance. Transient and bidirectional bias sweeps capture electrothermal hysteresis, gate-controlled switching latency, and bias-controlled recovery. Simultaneous activation of three gates lowers the switching threshold from about 104 $μ$A with all gates inactive to about 12 $μ$A, demonstrating cooperative suppression of superconductivity. The framework supports the design of nTron geometries, operating conditions, and multi-input architectures.

title: Pseudospin-mediated broadband hypersonic phonon transport beyond localized Berry curvature
summary: Phononic nanostructures offer compact and highly confined control of elastic waves for signal transport, filtering, and quantum transduction. More recently, topological phononic structures have been explored as a route to robust waveguiding around defects and sharp bends, offering a promising basis for scalable and reliable phononic circuitry. However, how robust transport can persist as conventional localized Berry-curvature signatures diminish with increasing structural perturbation remains elusive. Here, we demonstrate bend-resilient hypersonic phonon transport beyond the conventional valley Hall framework. Using an engineered propeller phononic crystal operating at 1.9 GHz, we continuously increase the geometric perturbation to gradually weaken the valley topology while enhancing modal pseudospin character. Strikingly, as the Berry curvature progressively delocalizes from valleys, the complete elastic bandgap broadens to a normalized width of 34% and the interface modes become more strongly confined. Two-port electromechanical measurements on a thin-film lithium niobate-on-SOI platform experimentally confirm broadband interface-mode transport with no measurable bend-induced loss, despite the absence of well-localized valley-topology signatures. Our findings establish modal pseudospin engineering as a powerful design principle for robust acoustic guiding beyond conventional topological constraints, paving the way for broadband hypersonic phononic circuitry for classical and quantum information processing.

title: Mathematical modeling of regime-dependent thermal response in multilayer wall assemblies with equal total steady thermal resistance
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Published version of the conference paper presented at the 78th International Conference on Vibroengineering, Lviv, Ukraine, October 2026
summary: Steady thermal resistance is a fundamental characteristic of building-envelope assemblies; however, equal steady resistance does not uniquely determine their transient thermal behavior. This study aims to numerically separate the effects of layer order, temperature-dependent thermophysical properties, and redistribution of thermal resistance between bulk and interfacial components in stationarily equivalent multilayer wall assemblies subjected to periodic and finite-pulse thermal loading. A one-dimensional transient heat-conduction model with Robin boundary conditions, finite interfacial thermal resistance, and source-supported temperature-dependent material properties was employed. All compared configurations were constrained to the same total steady thermal resistance at the reference temperature, $R_{\mathrm{tot}} = 3.65315$ m$^2$ K/W. The numerical implementation passed the adopted verification procedure with restrictions. The combined grid/time uncertainty was 0.325 %, below the prescribed 0.5 % acceptance criterion. For the tested pair differing only in layer order, the relative effect was -0.905 % for the periodic decrement factor and +0.566 % for the finite-pulse peak transmission ratio, with effect-to-uncertainty ratios of 79.2 and 88.9, respectively; the opposite signs therefore refer to two distinct regime-specific metrics. The temperature-dependent configuration produced a numerically resolved periodic effect of -2.005 %, whereas the corresponding pulse effect of -0.282 % remained below the adopted numerical-resolution threshold. For a compensated 5-10 % redistribution of bulk thermal resistance to interfacial contacts, the additional dynamic effect was likewise unresolved. The results demonstrate the value of controlled factor separation combined with explicit numerical-uncertainty assessment when evaluating transient thermal behavior.

title: Optimization of a Locally Shielded 16-Channel Transmit Array for Human Brain MRI at 10.5 T via Electromagnetic/Circuit Co-Simulation and Parallel Transmission Strategies
summary: Modern neuroimaging and neuroscience increasingly demand high spatial and temporal resolution, driving the use of ultrahigh-field (7 T and above) MRI for improved signal-to-noise ratio. Realizing this advantage depends critically on advanced radiofrequency (RF) and gradient technologies, particularly multi-channel transmit arrays and high-performance head-gradient systems. In integrated systems, a local RF shield must provide sufficient field confinement while preserving transmit performance and minimizing sensitivity to nearby conductive structures. In this work, we sought to optimize a locally shielded 16-channel transmit RF array for human neuroimaging at 10.5 T using electromagnetic/circuit co-simulation combined with parallel-transmission strategies. Candidate transmit-array and RF-shield configurations were evaluated before and after gradient-shield integration to identify a configuration with suitable RF transmit and shielding performance for the integrated system. The results show that no single standalone metric, including static RF shimming performance, dynamic parallel transmission (pTx) performance, or external-field leakage, reliably predicts robustness after gradient-shield integration. Progressive screening identified the aligned loop-folded dipole (LFD) array combined with a compact cylindrical shield featuring a conical top and three windows (160-mm radius and 70-mm window length) as the final configuration. Without RF-circuit retuning, the selected design maintained external-field leakage below 1% and after gradient shield integration achieved whole-brain excitation coefficient of variation (CoV) of approximately 27% with static RF shimming and 9% with dynamic pTx. Experimental validation of the unshielded LFD array showed good agreement between simulated and measured B1+ efficiency distributions, with a normalized root-mean-square error (NRMSE) of approximately 8%.

title: Statistical analysis of crossing beam speckle fields
comment: 17 pages, 8 figures. Submitted to Physical Review E
summary: Building on the statistical analysis of single beam speckles, this paper develops a statistical description of speckle fields formed by crossing laser beams. A formal definition of individual speckles and their domains allows us to quantify the effective size and abundance of speckles. For two crossing beams, the effective speckle size is derived from the local curvature of the intensity field, and the expected speckle abundance is found asymptotically with the Kac-Rice formula. Monte Carlo simulations of speckle abundance show excellent agreement with the theoretical abundance formula. The two beam speckle analysis is then applied to a symmetric quad beam configuration motivated by polarization smoothing and demonstrates that increasing the separation between beams reduces expected stimulated Brillouin scattering reflectivity from saturated speckles. The statistical model is then extended to an arbitrary number of beams using a coordinate free formulation to obtain the spectral density of laser driven electron density fluctuations.

title: Shower Shapes and Data-Driven Simulation Studies using a Highly Granular Crystal ECAL
summary: Electron shower shapes were measured using standard shower profile models for events observed with a highly granular crystal electromagnetic calorimeter prototype, with data taken from a 2025 test beam at the CERN Proton Synchrotron T9 beamline. The shower maximum, longitudinal shape parameter, and lateral variance were found to be well approximated by log-normal distributions. From these distributions, properties of the absorber were measured to be in agreement with existing literature. Energy-dependent correlations were observed between all parameters and most strongly between the shower maximum and the shower shape parameter. The distributions of energy and event-by-event pairwise log ratios of energy fractions in individual active volumes of the calorimeter conditional on the shower shape were found to be consistent with shifted and scaled Gamma and Fisher's-z distributions, respectively. Generative methods were developed to simulate the logarithm of shower shape variables using Gaussian copulas. Copula sampling for shower shape parameters was found to produce superior modeling of heavy tails observed for the shower maximum and longitudinal shape parameter distributions when compared to direct sampling from a correlated multivariate normal distribution. A copula method was also devised to sample full shower events conditional on the shower shape parameters by exploiting the observation that the vector of energy fractions follows a logistic Log-Gamma distribution, the joint relation implied by the observed Fisher's-z form of the pairwise log-ratios. The generative model was evaluated using standard manifold and classifier metrics and was found to approach the data-versus-data ceiling. The fastest generation time was found to be around 30 μs per particle shower.

title: Diagnosing internal leakage currents through magnetometry of lithium-ion cells
summary: Internal leakage currents are difficult to detect and to localize through measurements at the terminals of lithium-ion cells. We measured the magnetic fields of pouch cells non-invasively with a magnetometer while a battery cycler set the current and recorded the voltage. A three-axis magnetoresistive sensor remains fixed inside a three-layer magnetic shield, and two linear stages move the cell in two dimensions relative to the sensor to acquire a map of the magnetic field above the cell. The field of an intact cell was linear in current from 10 to 420 mA, and its maps were symmetric between charge and discharge. To create internal leakage currents, two 600 mAh cells were damaged by mechanical indentation. Both cells developed a magnetic field at zero applied current that decayed over hours, while the cell voltage showed a loss of charge by self-discharge. This field breaks the symmetry between the charge and discharge maps, which allows leakage to be detected while the cell is being cycled. At rest, the setup detects leakage currents down to about 1--3 mA. The results highlight opportunities for battery diagnostics and safety, and may help in designing techniques for characterizing soft shorts.

title: Deep-learning-enabled rapid spatially multiplexed wavefront sensing with a thin diffuser
summary: Conventional wavefront sensing typically measures aberrations along a single guide-star direction, limiting the correction of field-dependent aberrations over a wide field of view. Spatial multiplexing with a thin diffuser enables simultaneous measurements across multiple isoplanatic patches, but the computational cost of reconstruction makes it difficult to track changing aberrations. We propose a deep-learning approach that combines recurrent all-pairs field transforms for displacement estimation with Zernike coefficient regression. Experimental results show that the method accurately reconstructs multiple wavefronts from a single speckle pattern and reduces three-channel reconstruction time from 2801.6 ms with conventional digital image correlation (DIC) to 23.1 ms. The reconstructed wavefronts agreed more closely with sequential single-channel references than those obtained by multiplexed DIC, and simulations showed that Zernike regression was more robust to noise than direct gradient integration. These results suggest a path toward dynamic wide-field aberration sensing and high-speed adaptive optics.

title: Development of a low-level radio frequency system for remote in situ superconducting radio frequency cavity measurements and calibrations in conduction-cooling systems
summary: We developed a low-level radio frequency (LLRF) system for superconducting radio frequency (SRF) cavity measurements in a conduction-cooling system. A voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO) was used in a phase-locked loop (PLL) to track the frequencies of SRF cavity modes. {\tt{Python}}-based software developed in-house controlled and monitored the system. By introducing an additional circulator and associated components, we developed an LLRF system enabling fully remote in situ SRF cavity measurements for the first time. This design also enables remote in situ calibrations. Hence, our LLRF system improves safety through fully remote operation and enhances measurement precision through in situ calibrations, with safety always taking priority. These calibrations are important for measurements in conduction-cooling systems because temperature stability and uniformity in these systems are poorer than those in convection-cooling systems using costly liquid helium and can vary over time and with environmental conditions.

title: Partitioning and Merging in Phase Unwrapping: A Systematic Review of Methods and Evidence
summary: Phase unwrapping underlies radar interferometry, magnetic resonance imaging and optical metrology. When an image is too large or too difficult to unwrap in one piece, many methods cut it into units, unwrap each unit, and merge the results. To our knowledge, no systematic review had brought these partitioned methods together. This review gathers them, for two-dimensional images and three-dimensional volumes. It describes how the units are built: fixed tiles, adaptive tiles, regions computed from the data, or pieces imposed by the acquisition, such as subapertures, slices and scenes. It then classifies how the units are merged, in four classes: after each unit is unwrapped, through one integer per jump-free region, during the solve, or through an external reference. Three findings stand out: building the units and merging them are two separate decisions; the merging rule decides whether the merged phase stays congruent with the measured one; and most tests change both decisions at once, so few results show which one helps. We state what a study can report to support a claim on memory, speed or accuracy. Our aim is to document the methods, not to rank them. Following PRISMA 2020, four bibliographic databases (OpenAlex, IEEE Xplore, Web of Science and Scopus), searched on 1 October 2026, returned 1,800 records. After removing duplicates, screening titles and abstracts, adding a citation search and reading 298 full texts, we included 149 studies, published from 1987 to 2026. The review was not registered and received no specific funding.

title: Producing and Measuring Circularly Polarized X-rays: A Jones and Mueller-Stokes Treatment of Crystal Phase Plates
summary:
Converting a linearly polarized X-ray beam into a circularly polarized one, and then verifying the polarization state actually delivered, are standard operations at synchrotron radiation facilities. The key optical element is a quarter-wave plate (QWP), a birefringent crystal that introduces a 90-degree (quarter-wavelength) phase retardation between the two orthogonal components of the electric field.
  This paper presents a self-contained theoretical treatment of X-ray polarization optics. We first establish the Jones and Mueller-Stokes formalisms and their connection via the Pauli matrices, fixing the sign and handedness conventions explicitly and reconciling them with those used elsewhere in the literature. From there we derive the Jones and Mueller matrices of a general retarder at an arbitrary orientation angle chi (including the QWP that converts horizontal linear polarization into circular polarization of either handedness) and of linear polarizers, and describe the experimental Stokes polarimetry protocol used at synchrotron beamlines. These results are then combined to treat the general crystal phase plate, characterized by two complex reflection (or transmission) amplitudes r_s and r_p, obtaining the degree of circular polarization delivered for an arbitrary incident beam as a function of chi and the phase retardation delta. Finally, we turn to the practical implementation of these elements with perfect-crystal diffraction: the residual polarization impurity of a Brewster-angle polarizer and the role of ray tracing in evaluating it, and the choice of diffraction geometry (Bragg or Laue, diffracted or transmitted beam) for obtaining a significant, controllable phase shift. The formalism presented here is the mathematical background of the treatment of polarization in the ray-tracing code SHADOW4.

title: Carrier relaxation confines the Bogdanov--Takens degeneracy of an optically injected semiconductor laser
summary: Optically injected semiconductor lasers are forced nonlinear oscillators whose locking boundaries are organized by codimension-two points. We ask which property of the carrier balance permits or forbids a Bogdanov--Takens (BT) point in the standard three-dimensional rate equations. Taking the carrier inversion $n$ as distinguished observable, the rate that enters the spectral conditions is the slope of the gain--loss balance, $ξ=\partial\dot n/\partial n=-2Γ/κ$, where $Γ$ is the damping of the relaxation oscillation and $κ=1+2Bn$ the normalized stimulated-emission factor. The two BT conditions become affine in $ξ$ and imply the exact sum rule $K^{2}=I[1-(1+κ)I]$ between injection amplitude $K$ and intracavity intensity $I$. The product of the two relaxation eigenvalues that survive at a saddle-node is bounded below by $1-16Γ^{2}$, so that no BT point exists for $Γ<1/4$, whatever $B$, the linewidth enhancement factor, the injection strength and the detuning; below this barrier every contact between Hopf and saddle-node curves is a fold--Hopf point. For $B=0$ the barrier is completed to an exact existence criterion. We prove that the unfolding of a BT point by injection strength and detuning is transversal if and only if two explicit curves cross transversally in the plane of locked states; for $B=0$ this is a simple root of an explicit function, and transversality fails exactly at the existence threshold. Two BT points at $Γ=1/2$, $α=2$ are verified to be generic, and the contacts between Hopf and saddle-node curves are classified into fold--Hopf, BT and nilpotent triple-zero points.

title: MuSTRNG: A Muon-Based Synchronizable True Random Number Generation System
comment: This manuscript has been submitted to IEEE TNS for peer reviewing
summary: Cosmic-ray muons provide naturally occurring stochastic events detectable by spatially separated devices, offering a potential physical source for synchronized random-bit generation. This is possible because the same physical muons can be independently detected by both devices and used to derive corresponding random-bit segments. Therefore, identifying common muon events and correctly aligning the event sequences are essential for synchronized random-bit generation. This article presents MuSTRNG, a muon-based synchronizable true random number generation system with two synchronization methods: Tracking--Tracking and Tracking--Nontracking. For Tracking--Tracking synchronization, track-based screening removes events whose reconstructed tracks do not intersect the detector area of the other device; angle-based screening partitions reconstructed directions into angular bins and aligns the event sequences to remove inconsistent pairs; and timestamp-based screening compares higher-order timestamp bits to further suppress residual mismatches. Tracking--Nontracking synchronization applies track-based screening only at the tracking-capable device, followed by timestamp-based screening between the two devices. A prototype with two tracking-capable devices was evaluated. For Tracking--Tracking synchronization, the three-stage process reduced the invalid-event ratio to 0.28% using 15-bit random segments, while the generated bit sequences showed generally favorable results in the applicable NIST SP~800-22 tests. Reprocessing the data without track information from one device provided preliminary support for Tracking--Nontracking synchronization, yielding an invalid-event ratio of 0.30% using 5-bit random segments. These results demonstrate the feasibility of muon-based synchronized random-bit generation under different device configurations, with potential application to secure communications.

title: Diagnostically Meaningful, Privacy-aware Synthetic Chest CT via Class-Conditional Latent Sampling in Diffusion Autoencoders
summary:
Large, well-annotated datasets are essential for developing medical artificial intelligence models, yet data sharing is often restricted by privacy regulations. Synthetic images may help address this limitation if they preserve diagnostic information while reducing the risk of reproducing patient data. We developed a diffusion autoencoder-based framework for class-conditional synthetic chest CT generation that incorporates latent-space distance filtering to reduce the likelihood of regenerating training samples.
  A diffusion autoencoder was trained on the public RSNA 2020 Pulmonary Embolism (PE) dataset. PE-positive and PE-negative images were synthesized by sampling latent representations from class-specific kernel density estimates. Samples with a nearest-neighbor latent-space distance below a predefined threshold were rejected. To assess diagnostic utility, ResNet-50 classifiers were trained across 10 independent runs using real, synthetic, or mixed real-synthetic datasets. Performance was evaluated on a held-out real test set using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with DeLong 95% confidence intervals (CIs).
  Models trained on synthetic data achieved an AUC of 0.862 (95% CI, 0.851-0.874), only slightly lower than models trained on real data (AUC = 0.872, 95% CI, 0.861-0.883) and mixed real-synthetic data (AUC = 0.865, 95% CI, 0.855-0.876). These differences were statistically significant (p < 0.05) but small in absolute terms. A nearest-neighbor copy-detection analysis of 38,000 synthetic slices found no direct copies of real training images.
  These findings indicate that the synthetic CT images preserve diagnostically meaningful information for image-level PE classification while incorporating measures intended to enhance privacy awareness and reduce similarity to real patient data.

title: Tunable Terahertz Bandpass Filter based on the Photonic Emulation of a 2DEG Interferometer through the Geometric Phase of Light
summary: Terahertz frequencies are expected to become a key player in next-generation wireless communications. For this transition to occur seamlessly, tunable bandpass filters for channel selection are essential. However, conventional Fabry-Pérot cavity-based bandpass filters face inherent limitations. Specifically, their tunability is restricted by physical constraints, such as the maximum achievable mirror separation. In this work, drawing inspiration from electronic interferometers, we demonstrate a continuously tunable bandpass filter operating near 0.3 THz by exploiting the geometric phase of light, the Pancharatnam-Berry phase. Our device incorporates intracavity waveplates for polarization control and is described by a mathematical expression analogous to that of the electronic interferometer governed by the Aharonov-Bohm phase, thereby realizing a photonic analogue. Using custom-designed subwavelength waveplates and cavity mirrors, we achieve a finesse of $\mathcal{F}\approx17$, a quality factor of $Q\approx1.5\times10^{3}$, and a resonance linewidth of $Δf_{\mathrm{FWHM}}\approx 200$ MHz. Beyond terahertz communication technology, this system is expected to find applications in fields requiring high frequency resolution, such as spectroscopy.

title: Existence of single-resonance parametric bound states in the continuum: System of Schrödinger equations
summary: A bound state in the continuum (BIC) is an eigenmode of a linear wave system with its eigen-frequency embedded in the radiation continuum of scattering states. At the frequency of a BIC, scattering problems with given incident waves from infinity lose uniqueness. Due to their close connection with strong resonance effects, BICs have found many useful applications in classical and quantum wave systems. Existence theories of BICs have been established for some cases involving the so-called symmetry-protected BICs, Friedrich-Wintgen BICs, and Fabry-Perot BICs. The single-resonance parametric BICs (srp-BICs) are another important class of BICs. Such a BIC emerges from a single resonant state through tuning a real parameter. Using a simple system of two one-dimensional Schrödinger equations, we demonstrate the formation of srp-BICs and establish a rigorous existence theory.

title: Conformal Risk Control for Sentinel-1 Flood Maps under Event Shift and Local Recalibration
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures. Accepted for presentation at IEEE AGERS 2026. This is the submitted version. \c{opyright} 2026 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted. Permission from IEEE must be obtained for all other uses
summary: Conformal Risk Control (CRC) selects a threshold to limit missed labeled positives under exchangeability, but low omission risk can come at the cost of an excessively large flood map. We examine this trade-off with a frozen bi-temporal Sentinel-1 predictor, 403 expert-labeled source groups, and ten evaluable leave-one-event-out folds. At a target risk of 0.10, source-calibrated thresholds produce mean group losses of 0.1726 in Somalia and 0.1985 in Nigeria (four groups). The other eight folds select zero thresholds, labeling every valid pixel as flooded; their excess predicted area is 3.15-20.55 times the labeled positive area. Local threshold recalibration is feasible in 559 of 570 scheduled splits. The equal-event frequency of meeting the observed risk target with a positive threshold is 0.95% at ten labeled groups and 8.00% at twenty, using different predefined event pools. At fifty groups, exploratory recalibration meets both conditions in 24/30 Paraguay splits and none in India or the United States. Labels include permanent water, so the loss does not isolate newly flooded land. The results show why omission risk should be reported alongside mapped area, calibration feasibility, and event-specific outcomes.

title: Transport Layer-Driven Optimization of Color and Efficiency in TADF OLEDs for Large-Area Applications
summary: Balancing structural simplicity with high efficiency is crucial for practical applications of organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs), especially in large-area lighting devices. Optimizing the charge-transport layers in multilayer OLEDs controls the recombination zone within the emissive layer, thereby enhancing the device's performance. Herein, we experimentally and computationally investigate how the thicknesses of the electron and hole transport layers affect the performance of orange-red thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) OLEDs. Using a TADF emitter, 2-[4-(diphenylamino)phenyl]-10,10-dioxide-9H-thioxanthen-9-one (TXO-TPA), at 10 wt\% concentration in 4,4-Bis(N-carbazolyl)-1,1-biphenyl (CBP) host, we achieve a maximum external quantum efficiency ($η_{EQE}$) of 20.86\% and a peak luminance of 32,800 cd m$^{-2}$. Using a combination of drift-diffusion and optical simulations, we reveal how variations in hole- and electron-transport-layer thicknesses modulate the charge-carrier balance and shift the recombination zone within the emissive layer. This tuning not only optimizes exciton formation but also enables color tuning from green to red without altering the emissive material. Our findings highlight the critical role of transport layer engineering in achieving efficient, color-controlled OLEDs with simplified architectures. Furthermore, we successfully demonstrate a large-area OLED device (~20 cm$^{2}$), achieving an impressive $η_{EQE}$ of 17\%, underscoring the scalability and practicality of our approach for general lighting applications.

title: NeuroRefine: Six-Head MLP Content Conditioning and Qwen Refinement for Faithful fMRI Decoding
summary: Reconstructing seen images from fMRI has advanced through diffusion models, but the current state-of-the-art Brain-IT pipeline still has a lossy bottleneck: its low-level branch outlines the figure well, yet the diffusion model that follows frequently mispaints colour, object identity and layout. We move one step backward and condition the refiner directly on the fMRI-derived low-level image, using six one-hidden-layer MLP heads (scene, main-subject category, count, colour, object, layout) to predict the content prompt that guides a frozen Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 model. On the 930 shared NSD concepts, scored with Brain-IT's own metric code on the same ground truth, NeuroRefine reaches a CLIP image cosine of 0.755 against 0.735 for Brain-IT enhanced and produces markedly sharper images, while the saturated 2-way identification is unchanged. The low-level image supplies an explicit spatial prior rather than a lossless layout: refinement trades some layout agreement (0.541 against 0.638) for semantic fidelity and texture. We then show that the standard panel is multi-factor: a high PixCorr can coexist with completely different content, so we read the low-level and semantic factors separately and quantify where they disagree. Finally, we trace the cortical sources of the prompt heads across subjects and report their causal lesion profile and the fMRI noise ceiling. Direction errors are left to future work.

title: Ferroionic CuCrP2S6 Integrated Silicon Photonics for Neuromorphic Computing
summary: Neuromorphic photonic computing calls for optical states that combine stimulus accumulation, spontaneous relaxation, and nonvolatile state retention without continuous power dissipation. Here, we demonstrate a ferroionic photonic platform by integrating layered van der Waals CuCrP2S6 onto silicon microring resonators using a back-end integration process. Electrical pulsing produces unidirectional blue shifts in the optical resonance, consistent with field-driven redistribution of mobile Cu ions and giving rise to a history-dependent optical response. The resulting optical state is strongly pulse dependent, exhibiting both volatile and nonvolatile components. A short 20-pulse excitation produces an initial 70 pm resonance shift that relaxes toward baseline within approximately 60 s, with a volatile relaxation time constant of 27-29 s. In contrast, after 1000 pulses, an initial 0.27 nm resonance shift relaxes to a persistent 0.13 nm nonvolatile state that is retained for at least 24 h. Repeated 6 V electrical pulses produce a progressive resonance shift over 1000 cycles, demonstrating cumulative optical integration. A fixed-wavelength readout converts the accumulated resonance shift into a thresholded optical response, with the normalized transmission remaining above the selected threshold through 600 pulses and falling below it at the 800-pulse state. These dynamics realize the basis for a leaky integrate-and-fire photonic neuron, where the pulse-dependent ionic response provides integration, spontaneous relaxation supplies a passive leak, persistent states provide nonvolatile memory, and fixed-wavelength readout provides an optical threshold response.

title: PICE: Prototype-Informed Conditional Model Evolution Toward Self-Evolving Medical Image Recognition
summary: Medical image classifiers in clinical practice must continually evolve to accommodate emerging disease categories while maintaining reliable classification of existing conditions. This is challenging because privacy and data-sharing restrictions limit access to historical patient data, while assigning dedicated capacity to each new diagnostic task causes linear model growth. Effective evolution requires preserving prior disease knowledge without retaining historical images while expanding model capacity only when necessary. To this end, we propose PICE, a Prototype-Informed Conditional Model Evolution framework organized around what to preserve, when evolution is needed, and how that evolution is realized. PICE preserves prior disease knowledge in a prototype-statistical memory. For each incoming task, it assesses compatibility with historical references reconstructed from memory, reusing the closest adapter when compatibility is sufficient and instantiating a new one when evolution is required. PICE then realizes evolution by updating the memory and recalibrating the unified classifier with Gaussian pseudo features, thereby integrating new knowledge into the cumulative diagnostic space. During inference, memory-derived similarities guide task-agnostic adapter selection and fusion, enabling prediction over all learned disease categories. Experiments on Skin8, Kvasir-V2, and Path16 demonstrate the effectiveness of PICE across diverse clinical scenarios. On Skin8, PICE achieves a 7.60\% improvement in accuracy over the SOTA method on new tasks, while maintaining 71.10\% accuracy on previous tasks. It also reduces additional learnable parameters by 18.51\%. These results indicate that PICE improves classification while balancing knowledge retention, adaptation, and parameter growth, supporting continual model evolution as new diagnostic categories emerge without access to historical images.

title: Gradient Optical Diffraction Tomography Using Deep Learning-Assisted Amplitude Estimation
summary: Gradient Optical Diffraction Tomography (GODT) enables the non-invasive reconstruction of a spatial derivative of the 3D sample's refractive index distribution, providing enhanced sensitivity to subtle refractive index variations through gradient-based contrast. Implemented using lateral shearing interferometry (LSI), GODT benefits from a common-path architecture that provides environmental stability and high signal-to-noise ratio measurements. Unlike conventional optical diffraction tomography (ODT), which requires numerical integration of LSI-derived phase gradients to recover the object phase, GODT enables direct tomographic reconstruction from the LSI data. Notably, GODT requires derivatives of both the phase and amplitude of the object fields as input. While the phase derivative can be readily extracted from LSI data, the amplitude gradient cannot be directly retrieved. Thus, in the original GODT formulation, the amplitude gradient was assumed to be negligible, limiting the accuracy of the resulting 3D reconstruction. In this work, we introduce amplitude-informed GODT (AI-GODT), which employs physics-informed supervised deep learning to estimate the missing amplitude gradient based on accessible LSI data, specifically the fringe modulation. The proposed approach, applying a ResNet architecture and training on computer-generated data, is validated through numerical simulation and experimental measurements of both a well-characterized test object and primary neuronal cell culture, demonstrating the network's ability to generalize to diverse samples. We show that incorporation of the recovered amplitude gradient into the GODT reconstruction pipeline improves the 3D reconstruction quality, especially in its out-of-focus regions. The software and datasets are openly available to facilitate reproducibility and further development.

title: Interpreting Speckle Effects Through Neuron Interventions
summary: Speckle, the multiplicative noise inherent to synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imaging, reduces the performance of pretrained SAR models. We use interpretability methods to examine its effects inside pretrained vision models. We identify neurons that respond selectively to speckle and test whether correcting their activations improves reconstruction. We study SARMAE, an Earth observation model pretrained on a million-scale SAR dataset. Synthetic scenes with known reflectivity allow us to measure recovery precisely. The model contains 38 speckle-selective neurons that track speckle's value distribution. Restoring these neurons to their clean values does not improve reconstruction. Activation patching across layers shows that the first MLP has the largest restoration and injection effects. Within this layer, a different set of 64 neurons recovers 44.1\% of the correlation loss on held-out scenes. When the speckle-selective neurons are held at their noisy values, 96.5\% of this gain remains, while holding the values of three decoder heads removes 37.4\%. In an ImageNet-pretrained MAE, restoration is most effective in the third MLP block. On manipulated Sentinel-1 and Capella images, the same 64 neurons also improve reconstruction, whereas for land-cover classification, only restoring the entire first MLP yields a clear gain. The neurons that respond most to speckle are therefore not the ones the model uses to recover the scene.

title: Minimum Effective-Susceptibility Bounds for Arbitrary Polarization Transformations in Metasurfaces
summary: Metasurfaces are increasingly employed for sophisticated polarization transformations, including general unitary and nonunitary Jones operations. Despite substantial advances in analytical synthesis methods, inverse design of these transformations remains challenging. Here, we show that the particular mathematical structure of Jones polarization transformations makes optimal effective-susceptibility synthesis analytically tractable within the generalized sheet transition condition (GSTC) framework. For reciprocal, lossless dipolar metasurfaces, we establish exact feasibility and global minimum attainment, and derive sharp effective-susceptibility bounds for representative unitary and nonunitary transformations. We identify when magnetoelectric coupling lowers the minimum susceptibility, when it offers no resource advantage, and how the required material response depends on the prescribed polarization transformation. Applications to polarization rotations, tunable compensators, and polarization-state separation, including unambiguous discrimination, demonstrate sharp physical limits and material-resource trade-offs. These results provide geometry-independent theoretical benchmarks that can guide numerical inverse design and the selection of metasurface architectures.

title: Evaluating Cine and Tagged MRI-to-Speech Synthesis with Complementary Metrics and MRI-Free Controls
comment: Accepted for an invited oral presentation in the Deep Dive session of SPIE Medical Imaging 2027, Vancouver, February 2027. 10 pages, 4 figures, 1 table
summary: Relating tongue motion measured with dynamic MRI to the speech it produces could inform rehabilitation after glossectomy. Prior studies have translated cine or tagged MRI into log-mel spectrograms and used the two-dimensional Pearson correlation between predicted and recorded spectrograms (Corr2D) to quantify the acoustic information captured by each imaging modality. However, Corr2D has not been calibrated against MRI-free predictors that preserve basic acoustic structure. Our contribution is an evaluation framework for speech synthesis from cine MRI, tagged MRI and their combination; the synthesis network is held fixed. On identical leave-one-subject-out folds, we compare four trained input configurations with two MRI-free controls: a static mean-spectrum baseline and a time-aligned cohort template. Across 44 subjects (18 after glossectomy) producing two utterances, the cohort template, which never sees an MRI, reached a Corr2D of 0.745 and 0.664. The static baseline, which contains no timing, reached 87 to 89% of that score. No trained configuration outperformed the template on Corr2D, a cepstral distance or ESTOI; seven of the eight fell significantly short on Corr2D. For cine MRI this held across three positional encodings, an encoder temporal-attention module and a training objective matched to the metric. Cine and tagged MRI differed consistently within subjects, although the direction depended on the metric. Absolute Corr2D alone therefore does not show that a model recovers acoustics from the MRI. The two controls are a reusable method: any study can compute them from its own training recordings, so a model's margin over them measures what its images contribute.

title: Fourier-Transform Photothermal Spectroscopy with Transient-Lens Detection
summary: We demonstrate Fourier-transform photothermal spectroscopy using broadband supercontinuum excitation and transient-lens detection. The output of a Ti:sapphire oscillator is broadened in a photonic crystal fiber to generate the supercontinuum pump, which is converted into a phase-stable pulse pair with a controllable femtosecond delay using a birefringent interferometer. The absorption-induced heating from the pump generates a transient thermal lens in the sample, which is detected as a function of delay by an off-resonant 800 nm photothermal probe beam. Fourier transform of the interferometric photothermal response yields a frequency-domain signal corresponding to the sample absorptance spectrum weighted by the pump spectrum. After division by the measured pump spectrum, the reconstructed photothermal spectrum is compared with a direct frequency-domain linear absorption measurement to evaluate the accuracy of the reconstruction. This method combines Fourier-transform broadband excitation with thermal-lens readout, allowing broadband linear absorption spectra to be obtained from pump-induced refractive-index changes rather than from transmitted excitation intensity. We demonstrate the method on phloxine B.

title: SpiderSkel: Sub-Pixel Multi-Tangent 2D Skeletonization from Inscribed-Disc Geometry
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables, plus 6 pages of supplementary material. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Image Processing
summary: Skeletonization reduces a binary shape to a compact medial representation, but pixel-grid discretization perturbs the boundary-contact geometry underlying the medial axis, creating tension among connectivity, reconstruction fidelity, and skeleton compactness. SpiderSkel is a family of training-free two-dimensional skeletonization methods built on multi-tangent inscribed-disc geometry. A tie-aware exact Euclidean distance transform retains tied nearest boundary sites rather than collapsing them to a single label; medial candidates are localised to sub-pixel positions from the inscribed disc's tangent contacts, filtered by the angular span of those contacts, and completed by connectivity-aware refinement. Across nineteen public benchmarks comprising 11,323 images of shapes, retinal vessels, cracks and roads, and document images, a single operating point fixed across datasets yields skeletons that, on every image, have exact skeleton topology under the component/hole certificate, remain fully connected, and have exact per-object reconstruction topology. The three SpiderSkel variants are the only evaluated methods to satisfy all three properties across every category; within each category, every variant is Pareto-optimal with respect to all twenty-two baselines in strict sub-pixel reconstruction Dice versus reduction rate. Incremental engines for all three variants reproduce the skeleton of a complete recomputation exactly across 23,040 verified edit steps, with median update latencies of 15.4-18.1 ms per foreground edit and 4.3-4.4 ms per canvas edit, and speedups reaching 33.0-fold on canvas edits.

title: Unveiling gauge-invariant on-chip phases from light intensity
summary: Physics-informed digital twins fitted to output powers increasingly program photonic processors, but these powers do not fix the implemented phase, which determines how light from different inputs interferes. Here we show that a twin trained on intensities alone predicts the gauge-invariant phase of programmed transformations, and that this prediction can be used to program the phase. On a $12\times12$ mesh, with phases measured by interference protocols formed by the mesh itself, intensity-only and phase-aware programs from random starts reach the same intensity fidelity but phase fidelities of 0.690 and 0.996, both as predicted by the twin. The prediction holds for blocks up to $10\times10$. With coherent inputs, the programmed phase determines the outputs: phase-aware programming reduces the direction-of-arrival error of an on-chip Butler matrix from 29 degrees to 2.0 degrees. Power measurements alone thus yield a phase-calibrated model of the mesh, without phase data in training or optics beyond the chip.

title: PRISM: Perceptual Rate-Controllable Extreme Image Compression with Visual State-Space Models
summary: Generative codecs built on pretrained diffusion priors achieve high perceptual quality at ultra-low bitrates (below 0.05 bpp). However, most methods still require a separate model for each bitrate, and offer no control over the amount of detail synthesized. Their rate efficiency also depends on the entropy model, where Mamba-based state-space models (SSMs) have recently improved autoregressive context modeling. However, conventional SSM scans are not aligned with the decoding order, and each decoding pass restarts from an empty state, discarding context accumulated in previous passes. We propose PRISM, an extreme image compression method that addresses these limitations. A single model provides two continuous controls: a rate knob that traverses the rate-distortion curve and a realism knob that adjusts the level of detail synthesized. Its visual state-space (VSS) context model introduces a decode-order-aligned (DOA) scan, which predicts each latent from a state that summarizes all decoded context, and cross-tap state carry, which initializes each tap with a summary of the previous one. Experiments show that PRISM outperforms both variable-rate and fixed-rate codecs, requiring on average 22% less bitrate than the strongest baseline at equal FID while also achieving higher PSNR.

title: Producing and Measuring Circularly Polarized X-rays: A Jones and Mueller-Stokes Treatment of Crystal Phase Plates
summary:
Converting a linearly polarized X-ray beam into a circularly polarized one, and then verifying the polarization state actually delivered, are standard operations at synchrotron radiation facilities. The key optical element is a quarter-wave plate (QWP), a birefringent crystal that introduces a 90-degree (quarter-wavelength) phase retardation between the two orthogonal components of the electric field.
  This paper presents a self-contained theoretical treatment of X-ray polarization optics. We first establish the Jones and Mueller-Stokes formalisms and their connection via the Pauli matrices, fixing the sign and handedness conventions explicitly and reconciling them with those used elsewhere in the literature. From there we derive the Jones and Mueller matrices of a general retarder at an arbitrary orientation angle chi (including the QWP that converts horizontal linear polarization into circular polarization of either handedness) and of linear polarizers, and describe the experimental Stokes polarimetry protocol used at synchrotron beamlines. These results are then combined to treat the general crystal phase plate, characterized by two complex reflection (or transmission) amplitudes r_s and r_p, obtaining the degree of circular polarization delivered for an arbitrary incident beam as a function of chi and the phase retardation delta. Finally, we turn to the practical implementation of these elements with perfect-crystal diffraction: the residual polarization impurity of a Brewster-angle polarizer and the role of ray tracing in evaluating it, and the choice of diffraction geometry (Bragg or Laue, diffracted or transmitted beam) for obtaining a significant, controllable phase shift. The formalism presented here is the mathematical background of the treatment of polarization in the ray-tracing code SHADOW4.

title: Weakly Conditioned Diffusion Model Augmentation for Prostate Segmentation
summary: Deep learning models for prostate MRI segmentation often struggle to generalize when trained on limited heterogeneous data, leading to boundary errors and over-segmentation. We present an augmentation framework using mask-conditioned synthetic and diverse T2-weighted MRI volumes to improve boundary precision and reduce over-segmentation. We employ a 2.5D weakly mask-conditioned denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) via channel concatenation. The diffusion model conditions on stacks of adjacent binary masks from training folds. The model generates T2 volumes consistent with the conditioning anatomy while diversifying tissue appearance. We evaluate the proposed approach on two cohorts of data: (i) the LUND probe cohort (n=432) for strategy selection and training nnU-Net from scratch with a 23% synthetic data mix, and (ii) the Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) prostate cohort (n=32) evaluated with a 20% synthetic data mix. For the LUND cohort, we found that training an nnU-Net model from scratch with a 23% synthetic data mix reduced the mean false-positive voxels per case from 11,102 (baseline) to 10,757. On the MSD cohort, the augmented model with a 20% synthetic mix achieved a mean cross-validated Dice of 0.9094, improving over the baseline (0.8935) by 1.59 percentage points and reducing mean false-positive voxels by 23.1% (4,201 to 3,229). Experimental results on both these cohorts suggest that mask-conditioned DDPM augmentation can reduce over-segmentation errors and improve boundary adherence in data-constrained settings.

title: Solitons as conversion events in quadratic crystals
summary: In a $χ^{(2)}$ crystal with temporal walk-off and negligible dispersion, signal, idler and pump pulses obey the integrable three-wave interaction. For a pump of intermediate group velocity we describe each soliton as a conversion event: the fusion of a signal--idler pair into a pump pulse, or the decay of a pump pulse, at a definite depth in the crystal. The asymptotic $\mathrm{sech}$ pulses, usually treated with three separate $2\times2$ scattering problems, are the legs of the event, a single pole of the $3\times3$ problem. For one event we give the conversion curve in closed form and the minimum crystal length; for several events, the rule by which they displace each other. A pump pulse is unstable, and its growing mode is the tail of a decay event: a seed carrying a fraction $\varepsilon$ of the photons along this mode makes the pulse decay after $Γ^{-1}\ln(c_+/\varepsilon)$, with $Γ$ the conversion rate and $c_+$ of order one. Unmatched signal and idler pulses form the resonance of Kaup, Reiman and Bers; we show that it is a fusion followed by a decay, each within a conversion length, and give its pump photon number in closed form. Since the delay between the input pulses sets the depth of the vertex, these quantities can be read on the output face of a single crystal; we give the scales for periodically poled KTiOPO$_4$.

title: Arbitrarily Weak Losses Destroy Fractal Bandstructure in Temporal Fibonacci Quasicrystals
summary:
Lossless photonic crystals with weak refractive index contrasts block limited frequencies. However, the same materials arranged in a non-periodic Fibonacci quasicrystal block all but infinitely rare fractally-distributed frequencies. Similar analysis shows that weak quasiperiodic refractive index variation in time should achieve infinitely broadband gain.
  We demonstrate that any small experimental losses immediately destroy this effect. Our methods also provide smoothness and approximation theorems for the localisation lengths central to topology in spatial problems.

title: Theory of Observability of Voigt-Wave Propagation in a Homogeneous Dielectric Material
summary:
A Voigt wave can propagate in a dissipative anisotropic dielectric material when a 4$\times$4 propagation matrix is defective, as happens for a uniform plane wave along a singular axis, and the field depends on the propagation distance linearly as well as exponentially. Whether it is observable outside a slab of that material generally depends on whether the defectiveness is inherited by the 2$\times$2 reflection and transmission matrices, which are extracted from the 2$\times$2 blocks of a 4$\times$4 transfer matrix that relates the fields at the two faces of the slab. Explicit tests exist for each type of defectiveness, and a counting argument shows that excitation and observability co-occur at oblique incidence only for isolated combinations of constitutive parameters and slab thickness. Normal incidence is exceptional: Voigt-wave excitation then generally implies a defective transmission matrix for almost all thicknesses, which explains Voigt's 1902 experiment on andalusite. Numerical searches for andalusite, $β$-gallium oxide, terbium orthoaluminate
  in a magnetostatic field, and hexagonal boron nitride show that a Voigt wave may be excited without being observable and that a defective reflection or transmission matrix need not signal the excitation of a Voigt wave.

title: Tunable Terahertz Bandpass Filter based on the Photonic Emulation of a 2DEG Interferometer through the Geometric Phase of Light
summary: Terahertz frequencies are expected to become a key player in next-generation wireless communications. For this transition to occur seamlessly, tunable bandpass filters for channel selection are essential. However, conventional Fabry-Pérot cavity-based bandpass filters face inherent limitations. Specifically, their tunability is restricted by physical constraints, such as the maximum achievable mirror separation. In this work, drawing inspiration from electronic interferometers, we demonstrate a continuously tunable bandpass filter operating near 0.3 THz by exploiting the geometric phase of light, the Pancharatnam-Berry phase. Our device incorporates intracavity waveplates for polarization control and is described by a mathematical expression analogous to that of the electronic interferometer governed by the Aharonov-Bohm phase, thereby realizing a photonic analogue. Using custom-designed subwavelength waveplates and cavity mirrors, we achieve a finesse of $\mathcal{F}\approx17$, a quality factor of $Q\approx1.5\times10^{3}$, and a resonance linewidth of $Δf_{\mathrm{FWHM}}\approx 200$ MHz. Beyond terahertz communication technology, this system is expected to find applications in fields requiring high frequency resolution, such as spectroscopy.

title: Blind spatially varying PSF estimation for fluorescence microscopy
summary: Optical aberrations degrade fluorescence microscopy images and measuring the underlying point spread function (PSF) often requires dedicated acquisitions or isolated emitters. Here we introduce DeepBlur, a neural network that estimates spatially varying two-dimensional PSFs directly from single images of biological structures. Trained entirely on physical simulations spanning aberrations, illumination and noise, it adapts to diverse imaging conditions without requiring user-supplied optical parameters. Using a deformable mirror, we acquire 1,290 images and assess blind PSF estimates against independent references. DeepBlur estimates agree closely with these references and improve deconvolution of experimentally aberrated images. Local PSF estimation also enables correction of spatially varying defocus and improves random-illumination super-resolution reconstruction in biological tissue. Available through DeepInv, a napari plugin and a web demonstration, DeepBlur can be readily integrated into computational microscopy workflows.

title: A Reconfigurable Four-State Sensor Based on Orthogonal Thermal and Chemical Stimuli
summary: This article presents a novel four-state refractive index (RI) sensor based on distinct phases of palladium (Pd) and vanadium dioxide (VO$_2$), controlled by orthogonal thermal and chemical stimuli. This is a numerical, simulation-only study: all results are obtained from two-dimensional finite-element method (FEM) simulations. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first reported multi-state reconfigurable RI sensor tuned by external control. VO$_2$ serves as a phase change material (PCM) offering two thermally switchable phases with highly contrasting optical properties, while the hydrogen absorption property of Pd provides two additional phases. Combining these, four operational states are realized: (i) $α$-Pd/low-$T$ VO$_2$; (ii) $β$-PdH$_x$/low-$T$ VO$_2$; (iii) $α$-Pd/high-$T$ VO$_2$; and (iv) $β$-PdH$_x$/high-$T$ VO$_2$. Thermal crosstalk between Pd and VO$_2$ is mitigated through tungsten (W) doping of VO$_2$. This work further introduces conditional state sensitivity (CSS), a novel figure of merit quantifying the optical contrast between each state transition. The proposed sensor achieves a peak sensitivity of 2871 nm/RIU for the undoped reference configuration and 2798 nm/RIU for the practical W-doped device, together with a peak CSS of 16,872 nm/RIU, establishing it as a multi-state reconfigurable platform with reduced thermal crosstalk and potential applications in industrial safety monitoring and optical logic gates.

title: Voltage-Enhanced Photorefractive Hysteresis in Thin-Film Lithium Niobate Photonic-Crystal Cavities
summary: We observe voltage-enhanced photorefractive hysteresis in thin-film lithium niobate nanocavities, causing the resonance to appear at different wavelengths during increasing- and decreasing-wavelength laser scans. Their separation grows with bias magnitude and optical power, but depends weakly on scan speed over 1-200 nm/s. A quasi-static surface-trap model links voltage-biased carrier transport to asymmetric trapping, whose space-charge field shifts the resonance through the Pockels effect. The model captures this hysteresis across three cavities through switching between stable steady states. Space-charge feedback opposes further carrier separation, limiting the hysteresis gap. The model informs photorefractive mitigation and resonance control in integrated electro-optic devices.
